Ideally, each circuit would be identified, maintained, and tracked separately as different maintenance assets, a strategy that also helps isolate problems when a system component has repeated issues. For example, if a piece of equipment reports two compressor failures one month apart, it could be an indication that both compressors failed in the unit or that the same compressor failed twice. The latter should be studied carefully because it is a premature failure, while the former might be normal based on the life of the equipment. In many organizations, assets are tagged as part of the inventory to track the asset and its value. Asset tags are also used to determine when an asset will be retired or replaced. Often assets are tagged with barcodes and can be scanned during a routine building sweep to verify that the asset still exists or to attach service requests and repair reports. Figure 3 shows an example of a trackable asset tag. Each asset has a unique identification number, which can be translated to a barcode for easy scanning during inventory sweeps or maintenance logging. d.
